P.w: Opened in 2001 as the first Universal Studios park in Asia; one of Japan's most visited theme parks, with areas including The Wizarding World of Harry Potter and Super Nintendo World.

P.ad: 1-1-10 Kaigan-dori, Minato-ku, Osaka (Tempozan Harbor Village), Japan
P.w: One of Japan's largest aquariums, built around a 5,400-ton central Pacific tank holding a whale shark, with exhibits themed on the Pacific Rim.

P.ad: Tempozan Harbor Village, 1-1-10 Kaigan-dori, Minato-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A 112.5 m Ferris wheel beside Kaiyūkan in Tempozan Harbor Village, with a roughly 15-minute ride over Osaka Bay and the city skyline.

P.ad: Osaka Prefectural Government Sakishima Building, 1-14-16 Nanko-kita, Suminoe-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Observation deck 252 m up atop the Sakishima building (completed 1995), giving a 360-degree panorama of Osaka Bay; known for night views.
Head shrine of over two thousand Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, protecting travellers and sailors; its four main halls face west in the ancient Sumiyoshi-zukuri style.

P.n: Mozu Kofun Group — Daisen Kofun (Emperor Nintoku's Tomb)
P.w: Cluster of 5th-century keyhole tombs in Sakai, UNESCO World Heritage (2019) with the Furuichi group; Daisen Kofun, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is the largest grave in the world by area (~840 m with moats). The mound itself is off-limits.

P.ad: Daisen Park, 2 Mozu Yugumo-cho, Sakai-ku, Sakai, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Museum in Daisen Park tracing the history of the port town of Sakai, starting with the kofun tombs and artifacts excavated from them.

P.n: Expo '70 Commemorative Park & Tower of the Sun
P.w: Vast park on the grounds of the 1970 Japan World Exposition, the first in Asia; Tarō Okamoto's 70 m Tower of the Sun stands over the main entrance as its icon.
Forested valley just north of Osaka with a roughly 3 km riverside trail from Hankyu Minoo Station to the 33 m Minoo Waterfall; famous for autumn colours.
Mountain temple above Minoh known as the temple of victory, its grounds dotted with thousands of small red daruma dolls left by wishers.

P.ad: 10-1 Senri Expo Park, Suita, Osaka, Japan
P.w: One of the world's largest ethnology museums, inside the Expo '70 Commemorative Park, with a huge exhibition of everyday artifacts from cultures around the world.
Hands-on museum in Ikeda, birthplace of instant ramen (Momofuku Ando, 1958); at My Cup Noodles Factory visitors design a cup and pick their own soup and toppings.
Widely considered Japan's finest surviving feudal castle — the white 'White Heron' keep is a National Treasure and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1993).
Hillside district where foreign merchants and diplomats settled after Kobe port opened in the 19th century; dozens of Western-style mansions (ijinkan) survive, many open as museums.
Waterfront park on reclaimed land in Kobe's port, home to the red 108 m Kobe Port Tower (1963), the Kobe Maritime Museum and the Earthquake Memorial.
Shopping and entertainment waterfront between JR Kobe Station and the port, popular at night for its harbour views.

P.ad: Sakaemachi-dori / Motomachi-dori, Chuo-ku, Kobe, Hyogo, Japan
P.w: The biggest Chinatown in western Japan, packed with more than 100 shops and restaurants and street-food stalls.
One of Japan's oldest shrines, said to be founded in the 3rd century by Empress Jingū; the name Kobe derives from 'Kanbe', the families who served it.
One of Japan's three most famous hot springs, over Mount Rokko from central Kobe; known for its iron-rich 'kinsen' gold and clear 'ginsen' silver waters, explorable on foot.
Four waterfalls (the tallest, Ontaki, 43 m) a short walk from Shin-Kobe Station; the Nunobiki Ropeway climbs above them to one of Japan's largest herb gardens.
The 931 m high point of the Rokko range behind Kobe, with panoramic views over Kobe and Osaka, especially at sunset and night.
Spanning the Akashi Strait to Awaji Island, it was long the world's longest suspension bridge (central span 1,991 m).

P.ad: Nada-gogo, Higashinada-ku / Nada-ku, Kobe, Hyogo, Japan
P.w: Japan's top sake-producing district; several breweries run shops, tasting rooms and brewing museums open to the public.
Kōbō Daishi's mausoleum at the end of a cemetery path through ancient cedars lined with over 200,000 graves; part of the UNESCO 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range'.
Head temple of Shingon Buddhism on Mount Kōya, founded by Kōbō Daishi in the 9th century; within the Kii Mountains UNESCO site.
Reconstructed castle keep on a hill in central Wakayama with free Nishinomaru garden and the maple-filled Momijidani garden and covered wooden bridge.
Castle-town keep (burned 1827, rebuilt 1954) halfway between Osaka and Wakayama, with 360-degree views over Osaka Bay; the town is famous for the Danjiri float festival.
Bayfront district one stop from Kansai Airport with the 256 m SiS Rinku Tower (Rinku Gate Tower Building), Rinku Premium Outlets (200+ shops) and Aeon Mall.

P.n: Kansai Airport Observation Hall Sky View
P.w: Observation hall at Kansai International Airport with 360-degree runway views, an aviation shop and the Sky Museum.
Japan's oldest operating amusement park ('Hira-Par'), with around 40 attractions including the ~80 m Sky Walker Ferris wheel.
6th-century keyhole mound believed to be the true tomb of Emperor Keitai; unusually open to walk on, with replica haniwa on display and the Imashirozuka Ancient History Museum next door.

About a quarter of Taishō Ward's residents have Okinawan roots, descendants of WWI-era migrant textile workers; Okinawan restaurants and shops cluster near JR Taisho Station and along the Hirao shopping street.
Nine walled Edo-style gardens built in 1992 on the site of former samurai residences beside Himeji Castle's west moat.

P.n: Umeda Sky Building — Kuchū Teien Floating Garden Observatory
P.ad: Umeda Sky Building, northwest of JR Osaka Station, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The 173 m twin-tower skyscraper (1993) joined at the top by the open-air Floating Garden observation deck — 360° views over Osaka, open till 22:30.
Temma's shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, god of learning, at the head of Tenjinbashi-suji; home of the Tenjin Matsuri.
The national mint where Japan's coins are struck; famous for opening its riverside avenue of cherry trees to the public each spring.

P.ad: HEP Five, east of Hankyu Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A red Ferris wheel bursting from the roof of the HEP shopping complex in Umeda — 106 m high, with views over Kita.
Hideyoshi's 1583 castle, rebuilt in 1931 — the main keep (a museum with a top-floor lookout) rises from stone walls and moats in a vast park famous for plum and cherry blossom.
The canal-side heart of kuidaore Osaka: neon, mechanised signs (the Glico Running Man, the Kani Doraku crab) and street food that barely closes.
"Osaka's Kitchen": a several-hundred-metre covered arcade of fishmongers, butchers, greengrocers and grill-it-on-the-spot stalls.
Osaka's premier shopping street — a ~600 m covered arcade mixing chain stores, boutiques and department stores, running north from Dōtonbori.
Osaka's answer to Harajuku: thrift stores, cafes and youth fashion around Triangle Park, west of Mido-suji.
The 'New World' district built after the 1903 Expo — half Paris, half Coney Island — around Tsūtenkaku, the 103 m tower rebuilt in 1956; the home of Osaka kushikatsu.
Founded by Prince Shōtoku in 593 — one of Japan's oldest temples and the first built by the state, with its five-storey pagoda on the classic straight-line layout.

P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Osaka's city zoo (1915) in Tennōji Park, below Tsūtenkaku.

P.n: Osaka City Museum of Fine Arts
P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The 1936 municipal art museum in Tennōji Park, with Keitakuen garden behind it.
Opened 2001 in a tower beside NHK Osaka, across from the castle: large-scale models chronicle the city from its days as Japan's first capital to the early Shōwa era, with views over the castle park.
Contemporary Japanese and international art on two underground floors of Nakanoshima; the 2007 building's entrance structure is designed to evoke growing bamboo.
Hands-on science museum and planetarium on Nakanoshima, next to the National Museum of Art.
The city art museum that opened on Nakanoshima in February 2022 — modern and contemporary art and design, part of the island's museum cluster.
Claimed as Japan's longest covered shopping street — 2.6 km of shops and eateries running north from the Tenmangū approach.

A moss-covered Fudō Myōō statue that worshippers splash with water, beside two 80 m stone-paved alleys of old kappo counters, bars and okonomiyaki shops — the setting of Oda Sakunosuke's 'Meoto Zenzai'.
Osaka's Akihabara: electronics, anime, games and maid cafés along Sakaisuji in Nipponbashi.
Osaka's grown-up entertainment quarter just south of Osaka Station — hundreds of restaurants, hostess bars and counters.
A pocket of pre-war row houses east of Umeda whose narrow lanes are now full of cafés, craft shops and vintage stores.
Osaka's oldest tutelary shrine, an Engishiki-listed great shrine to the land deities Ikushima and Tarushima, on the Uemachi ridge near Tanimachi 9-chōme.

P.ad: Osaka Castle Park, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: Shrine inside Osaka Castle Park enshrining Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Hideyori and Hidenaga as deities of success — a branch of Kyoto's Toyokuni Shrine.
Jon Jerde's 2003 mall on the old Osaka Stadium site, shaped like a canyon of rock strata, with ~70,000 plants on its terraced rooftop Parks Garden.
Japan's largest Koreatown: about 150 grocers, kimchi and chijimi stalls, restaurants and hanbok shops along a 300 m shopping street in Ikuno, a short walk from Tsuruhashi's yakiniku alleys.
The nation's most prestigious stage for bunraku, Osaka's own puppet theatre — runs of about three weeks in January, April, June, July/August and November.
The Umekita redevelopment beside JR Osaka Station — a large urban park with new towers opening in stages through spring 2027, next to the Grand Front Osaka complex.
Open lawns and reconstructed platform bases across from Osaka Castle Park marking the 7th–8th-century imperial palace of Naniwa-kyō, when Osaka was Japan's capital.
The ~300 m skyscraper that opened in 2014 — department store, hotel, art museum and the Harukas 300 observation deck with panoramic views across Osaka.

P.ad: Tennōji Park, Chausuyamacho, Tennoji-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: A 19,800 m² strolling pond garden behind the city art museum, designed by tea master Kizu Issai and built by Ogawa Jihei VII (of Heian Shrine and Murin-an fame); entry is just ¥150.
The park holding the zoo, greenhouse, art museum and Keitakuen, fronted by 'Tenshiba' — a Good Design Award-winning lawn with cafés a short walk from Tennōji Station.
Some 800 stalls in the warren beside Tsuruhashi Station — yakiniku, kimchi and Korean groceries, fresh fish and offal hot-pots; the smell of grilling meat greets you on the platform.

P.n: Ebisubashi & the Glico Running Man sign
P.ad: Ebisubashi bridge, Dōtonbori, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
P.w: The bridge over the Dōtonbori canal where everyone poses with the Glico Running Man — the neon heart of Minami's mechanised signs.

Famous for its 12 m-high lion-head stage, whose gaping mouth swallows bad luck and brings victory in competition; the shrine was rebuilt after the 1945 air raids and keeps an intangible-folk-culture tug-of-war rite.
Yoshimoto's 858-seat 'hall of laughter', Japan's largest comedy theatre — Yoshimoto Shinkigeki, manzai and rakugo 365 days a year.
Shinsekai's 130 m covered alley of kushikatsu and doteyaki counters and old game parlours, running south toward Dōbutsuen-mae.
A 150 m arcade of professional kitchen-supply shops — knives, plastic food samples, lanterns, signs and tableware — three minutes from Namba Station.

F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand (new for 2026) Chinese restaurant whose Hong Kong- and Guangzhou-trained chef serves Sichuan-style mouth-watering chicken and dim sum such as steamed dumplings and pork shumai.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) counter-style French restaurant run single-handedly by a seasoned chef, carrying forward classical French cuisine with boldness; named after the film Diva.

Michelin Bib Gourmand (new for 2026) retro bistro hung with French pop posters in a nine-tsubo space; standards include oeufs mayonnaise, pâté de campagne and beef cheek stewed in red wine, plus pasta, in generous sharing portions.
Michelin-selected (2026) kappo opened by an izakaya chef as a sister shop: creative omakase with salty, sake-friendly dishes, wrapping up with seasonal takikomi-gohan or curry rice with free refills.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant whose chef trained in Hozenji Yokocho and now cooks cuisine of the "here and now", mindful of how knife technique affects the flavour of sashimi.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant in an old family home, run by affable owner-chef Koji Kawahara whose menu abounds with ingenuity (distinction not confirmed in search).
One MICHELIN Star (2026): counter-style Chinese cuisine in which owner-chef Akihito Shintani works Osaka and Kansai ingredients and Kansai food culture into Chinese cooking — "kamigatachuka".
Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen shop whose signature soy-sauce ramen rests on a chicken broth of guinea fowl and free-range chicken raised together by a like-minded farmer.
One MICHELIN Star Japanese restaurant in Tamatsukuri, Tennoji-ku.
Two MICHELIN Stars (newly promoted in the 2026 guide, the only new two-star in Osaka): Japanese cuisine in Ueshio.
Michelin Guide-listed unagi (freshwater eel) restaurant in Katamachi, Miyakojima-ku.
Michelin Guide-listed charcoal yakitori grilled by a former Japan bantamweight boxing champion who took up yakitori as his second "ring"; the name evokes the "royal road" of yakitori.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi counter: fish is selected at Tsuruhashi Market and the nigiri are formed small so you can sample as many items as possible.

Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant; chef Tomonori Matsumura trained at a ryotei and in France, and his creed is to make ingredients taste even more like themselves — shrimp dishes use reduced shrimp stock.

Michelin Guide-listed yakitori built on premium Hinai-jidori chicken; the set menu blends techniques learned at Yakitori Ichimatsu with creative dishes like chicken shumai and confit, ending with takikomi-gohan or ramen.

Michelin Guide-listed yakitori where Hiroki Matsuoka ages Kagoshima free-range chicken and brushes skewers with a fragrant oil of his own, interspersed with soups and fried chicken dishes; meals end with earthenware-pot rice or chicken-broth ramen.

Michelin Guide-listed sushi counter of hinoki cypress: two kinds of sushi rice for harmony with toppings, soy-marinated tuna wrapped in nori tekkamaki-style — Edomae at heart with respect for Kansai culture.
One MICHELIN Star (2025 guide) Japanese counter where years of experience show in skilful work at counter and grill, convivial conversation and creative preparation.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) in Kitashinchi: creative kushiage that incorporates culinary influences from many countries — the sheer variety is endlessly fun.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) Chinese restaurant in Nishitemma.
Michelin Bib Gourmand: omakase-only Japanese cooking using fermented seasonings, no-nonsense dishes mixed with bar snacks that express the owner-chef's unaffected personality.
Michelin Guide-listed kushiage counter whose chef focuses on seafood in his kushikatsu prix fixe, frying tiger prawn rare to draw out its sweetness.
Michelin Guide-listed Kitashinchi kushiage that works extravagant ingredients such as foie gras, truffles and caviar into its skewers.

Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025 guide) shokudo in a detached Kitashinchi house hung with criss-crossing poles evoking Wakayama's Oto Fire Festival torches; expect gingered chicken liver, potato salad, deep-fried horse mackerel and seasonal dishes.
Michelin-selected (2026): an omakase set meal of tempura fried by the owner-chef, interspersed by the proprietress with dashi-simmered takiawase and hand-made oden.
One MICHELIN Star (2026) Naniwa kappo whose mission is cuisine matched to the guest; the menu, 'Yuno's omakase', strays freely from the norms of Japanese cuisine.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi shop turned from a delivery business into a counter by an Edomae-trained owner; sushi is served omakase, chosen to suit each guest's preferences.
Michelin-selected (2026) sushi restaurant in Ikutama, Tennoji-ku.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025 guide) soba house with Oribe stoneware and earthen walls, serving two kinds of soba: fine-ground seiro and coarse-ground inaka.
Michelin-selected (2026) casual Italian eatery with traditional fare chalked on a blackboard — tripe stewed in tomato, marlin baked in herb-seasoned breadcrumbs, mushroom pappardelle.
One MICHELIN Star (2026) Japanese restaurant in a refined modern sukiya-style space: sashimi that showcases the chef's knife skills and grilled dishes over bincho charcoal.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi counter near Shitennoji temple.

Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) French bistro named 'at the setting sun' for the couple's Lyon apprenticeship and Yuhigaoka; the chef cooks, his pâtissière wife serves, and portions are generous with vegetables in abundance.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2025 guide) kappo izakaya run by a sake-loving couple — he cooks, she warms the sake — with a seafood-dominated menu crafted to double as bar snacks.

F.ad: 1F, Shin Daibiru, 1-2-1 Dojimahama, Kita-ku, Osaka 530-0004, Japan
F.w: Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant; Toshihiro Shimizu studied agriculture to know all he could about ingredients and taught himself to craft his own menu.
Three MICHELIN Stars (2026): exceptional Japanese kaiseki cuisine in the Senriyama residential district of Suita.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant whose chef, intent on breathing novelty into Japanese cuisine, pays tribute to the restaurant where he apprenticed.
One MICHELIN Star (2026) French restaurant in a residential corner of Toyonaka: open kitchen and counter seating, with cuisine based on classics learned during the chef's Paris apprenticeship.
Three MICHELIN Stars (2026): a planet-like artwork of overlapping dishes forming the Earth dominates the dining room, and "Dialogue with the Earth" is the theme of the cuisine.
Three MICHELIN Stars (2026): 'Taian' means 'big hut' — modest, clean décor, with Japanese cuisine that crystallises the skill and passion of Hitoshi Takahata.

One MICHELIN Star (2025 guide): Hiroaki Osawa cooks Chinese food in sync with the Japanese seasons, starting from ingredients piled on a large plate — e.g. drunken crab with baked apple, and pears with roast wagyu fillet and chilli oil.

Michelin Guide-listed Kitashinchi restaurant ranging from old-school Japanese to creative Western dishes; grilled celery with vinegar-miso, bite-sized beef cutlets and crab cream croquettes are year-round favourites.
Michelin One Star (2026) Kitashinchi branch of Senriyama's Kashiwaya, offering ryotei service in a counter setting.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi counter in Kitashinchi.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Tenjimbashi.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Ikedacho, Kita-ku.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Tenjimbashi.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Fukushima.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Sugaharacho, Kita-ku.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Sennichimae.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Tenjimbashi.
Michelin One Star (2026) sushi counter in Kitashinchi.
Michelin Guide-listed sushi restaurant in Abeno.
Michelin One Star (2026) innovative restaurant expressing the natural deliciousness of each ingredient through creative combinations.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant: tradition-respecting monthly menus with playful touches; modern counter plus five private rooms.

F.ad: 5F, The Ritz-Carlton, Osaka, 2-5-25 Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka 530-0001, Japan
F.w: Michelin Guide-listed tempura restaurant on the 5F of The Ritz-Carlton, Osaka.
Michelin Guide-listed Naniwa (Osaka) kappo-style Japanese restaurant mixing classic grilled/simmered dishes with creative spins.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant serving rice cooked in earthenware pots.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2023 guide) kushiage restaurant with uniquely inspired deep-fried skewer set menus.
Michelin One Star (2026) Japanese restaurant using seafood delivered directly from Ishikawa.
Michelin One Star (2026) Japanese restaurant in Shinsaibashisuji.
Michelin Two Stars (2026) Japanese restaurant; chef-owner Masamitsu Hisano sources the finest seasonal produce from across Japan.
Michelin One Star Japanese restaurant whose seasonal-themed hassun platters are the star attraction.
Michelin One Star (2026) Japanese restaurant upholding Osaka traditions with new influences.
Michelin One Star (2026) tempura restaurant in Nishitemma.
Michelin One Star (2026) Japanese restaurant in Nishitemma.
Michelin Guide-listed yakitori restaurant serving prix fixe menus of Kyushu chicken.
Michelin One Star (2026) Japanese restaurant in the Osaka kappo tradition.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese restaurant weaving Japan's culture and traditional ceremonies into its menu.
Michelin Guide-listed steakhouse grilling heifer-only Japanese Black wagyu by bincho flame and far-infrared heat.
Michelin Guide-listed Japanese shokudo with monthly-changing prix fixe; gyudon recalls its late-night-eatery days.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) ramen shop in Katsuyama, Tennoji-ku.
Michelin One Star Japanese restaurant in Temma.
Michelin Two Stars (2026) Japanese restaurant in Tenjimbashi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tempura restaurant in Tenjimbashi.
Michelin Guide-listed Spanish restaurant in Azuchimachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand kushiage counter: around 25 kinds of skewers are usually on, from classic to Korean kimchi, Indian curry and Italian tomato-sauce versions.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon house in Fukushima.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon shop in Nishitenma.

F.ad: B2F Osakaekimae Daisan Bldg, 1-1-3 Umeda, Kita-ku, Osaka 530-0001, Japan
F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand udon flagship in the Ekimae Building basements by Osaka Station.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon shop near Nakazakicho.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon shop on the Tenjinbashi side of Ogimachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand udon in the Hiranomachi office district.
Michelin Bib Gourmand chūka-soba shop on the Uemachi plateau near the castle.

F.ad: B2F Semba Center Bldg Sangokan, 1-4-3 Sembachuo, Chuo-ku, Osaka 541-0055, Japan
F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen in the Semba Center Building basement.
Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen by Minamimorimachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba off Tenjinbashi-suji.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba in Tanimachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba in Nishitenma.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba near Nagahoribashi/Tanimachi 6-chome.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba house in Dōjima.
Michelin Bib Gourmand soba in Nishitenma, an Osaka buckwheat institution.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tonkatsu in Shimanouchi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tonkatsu in Senbayashi shōtengai country.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tonkatsu in the Semba business district.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tonkatsu in Kyōmachibori, west of Honmachi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) tempura counter in Abeno.
Michelin Bib Gourmand izakaya in Fukushima, Osaka's izakaya neighbourhood.
Michelin-listed yakitori in Dōjima.
Michelin-listed yakitori counter in Dōjima/Kitashinchi.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) teppanyaki bar in Honmachi where the owner-chef's creative griddle dishes end, in true Osaka style, with pork or mixed okonomiyaki.
Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026): stylish, bar-like Kitashinchi teppanyaki on polished iron and copper griddles — okonomiyaki standards through creative tonpeiyaki, with Italian wines.
Michelin Bib Gourmand mixing French-bistro cooking with the teppan in Nishi-ku; known for its cabbage steak, and the meal ends with Osaka okonomiyaki.
Michelin Bib Gourmand okonomiyaki house near Higobashi — the konamon canon at Michelin-vetted value.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand for 2026 — a Thai kitchen in retro Nakazakichō.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand ramen shop for 2026 in Momodani, Ikuno.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand yakitori for 2026 in Nishitemma — charcoal-grilled chicken skewers.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand yakitori for 2026 in Miyakojima — skewers over binchō charcoal.
New Michelin Bib Gourmand for 2026 in Higashinari-ku: a neighbourhood Japanese spot built around sake and its snacks.

Selling takoyaki beside Amemura's Triangle Park since 1974 — crisp, light-brown shells with runny centres, a seven-ingredient dashi batter, and credited as the shop that started the mayonnaise lattice.
The Dōtonbori stand behind the giant 3D takoyaki ball: batter blended with dashi and milk, cooked ten minutes to a crisp shell and creamy middle.
Standing-only kushikatsu bar in the Shin-Umeda Shokudōgai by Umeda Station: grab crisp skewers off the trays and dip them (once) in the communal sauce.
The 1929 original of Osaka kushikatsu at the foot of Tsūtenkaku, credited with popularising the 'no double-dipping' sauce rule; skewers from staple beef to local-favourite red pickled ginger.
The Sennichimae flagship of Wanaka, a Michelin-recognised takoyaki maker (per Lonely Planet) and Cathay's and Inside Osaka's pick for the dish in Namba.
An Osaka noodle institution in business since 1864, famous for its Sasame Udon under a thick ankake sauce — picked by both Time Out and the Japan Konamon Association.
Founded in 1933 and credited as the shop that invented takoyaki — small, bite-size balls seasoned in the batter and eaten by hand, no sauce needed.
Spanish restaurant near Uehommachi 6-chōme ('Ueroku') named a new Michelin Bib Gourmand in the Kyoto Osaka 2025 guide.
Kyomachibori izakaya named a new Michelin Bib Gourmand in the Kyoto Osaka 2025 guide.
Tempura counter in Shimanouchi, added to the Michelin Guide Osaka in December 2025.
Dōjima tempura counter, a December 2025 addition to the Michelin Guide Osaka.
Italian osteria in Nishitemma, added to the Michelin Guide Osaka in December 2025.

F.ad: 37F, Four Seasons Hotel Osaka, 2-4-32 Dojima, Kita-ku, Osaka 530-0003, Japan
F.w: Chinese restaurant on the 37th floor of the Four Seasons Osaka in Dōjima, added to the Michelin Guide Osaka in December 2025.
Wagyu-focused Chinese cooking (wagyu chūgoku-sai) in Dōjimahama, added to the Michelin Guide Osaka in December 2025.
The Senba udon house credited with Osaka's kitsune udon, born here in the Meiji era: a large sweet-and-spicy simmered fried tofu over udon in gentle dashi (from ¥650).

F.ad: Namba Center Street, Namba, Chuo-ku, Osaka, Japan
F.w: Opened in Minami in 1910 as Osaka's first Western-style restaurant; its sweet-and-spicy curry, pre-mixed with the rice and crowned with a raw egg, is unchanged since the founding.
Osaka's most renowned butaman maker — the steamed pork bun every domestic traveller carries home; this is the Namba main store of the city-wide chain.
Fukushima tempura counter listed in the Michelin Guide Osaka.
Italian restaurant in Shimmachi named a new Michelin Bib Gourmand in the Kyoto Osaka 2025 guide.
